result: The authors generated a Tph1-bacTRAP mouse line to label EC cells and validated it by showing that GFP+ cells co-localize with 5-HT immunoreactivity (all in duodenum, >95% in jejunum and large intestine) and express EC markers Tph1, Chga, and Chgb at high frequencies by scRNA-seq. The most significant transcriptomic distinction was observed between small intestinal and colonic EC cells.
evaluation: Reviewers describe the transcriptomic data as 'solid' and 'more granular than previous data sets,' indicating acceptance of the Tph1-bacTRAP model validation and the regional transcriptomic distinctions. No concerns were raised about the specificity or quality of the reporter line or the scRNA-seq profiling.

result: Using unsupervised clustering, the authors resolved 14 EC subpopulations that were mostly demarcated by intestinal region (duodenum clusters 1-6, jejunum 7-10, proximal colon 11-12, distal colon 13-14). Small intestinal EC cells displayed a continuum in tSNE space, while colonic EC cells formed distinct clusters. The transcriptome diversity of EC cells is closely related to their spatial distribution along the rostro-caudal axis.
evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge the transcriptomic data as 'solid' and note that it 'will guide future research,' indicating acceptance of the 14-cluster resolution and regional organization. The editor states 'the evidence supporting the authors' claims is solid,' affirming the clustering results.

result: The authors resolved a second layer of EC cell complexity along the crypt-villus axis in the small intestine. Crypt clusters (4/5 in duodenum, 8/9 in jejunum) were distinguished from villus clusters (2/3/6 in duodenum, 10 in jejunum) based on differential expression of Tac1/Ucn3/Trpa1 (crypt-enriched) versus Sct/Cartpt/Trpm2 (villus-enriched), validated by smRNA-FISH. GO analysis revealed functional specialization: crypt clusters enriched for metabolism/detoxification, villus clusters for host defense.
evaluation: While reviewers accept the transcriptomic data as solid, one reviewer specifically notes that 'the proposed villus/crypt distribution of the 14 cell types is not verified adequately' and states 'the RNAscope and immunohistochemistry samples presented do not allow assessment if this interpretation is correct.' The reviewer suggests spatial transcriptomics would help verify this claim, indicating uncertainty about the crypt-villus assignments.

result: The authors identified a rare multihormonal EC cell population (cluster 6) in the duodenal villi, representing <0.1% of total duodenal epithelial cells. These Cck+/Tph1+/Oc3+ cells co-express multiple hormones (Sct, Ghrl, Gcg, Nts) and show spatial progression: Cck+/Oc3+ cells in crypts gradually acquire Tph1 expression as they migrate to villi, where triple-positive cells are more frequent.
evaluation: Reviewers describe the manuscript as focusing on 'a multihormonal cell type shown to express markers of pathogen/toxin and nutrient detection in the proximal small intestine,' indicating acceptance of this cluster 6 characterization. The data are described as 'solid,' and no concerns were raised about the identification or validation of this rare population.

result: Cluster 6 Cck+/Tph1+/Oc3+ cells are enriched with a dual molecular signature: pathogen/toxin recognition molecules (Crp, Tlr2, Tlr5) and nutrient sensing receptors (Mc4r, Casr). Over 85% of Mc4r+ or Casr+ cells co-expressed pathogen/toxin recognition genes. The authors suggest these cells may react to gastric content entering the duodenum and play a role in gut defense mechanisms.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly note the manuscript focuses on this 'multihormonal cell type shown to express markers of pathogen/toxin and nutrient detection,' indicating acceptance of the dual sensory signature. The data are described as 'solid,' and no concerns were raised about the molecular characterization or functional interpretation of these cells.

result: In the proximal colon, EC cells encompassed two clusters: cluster 11 (Iapp+/Cpb2+/Serpine1+/Sct+) involved in coagulation regulation, and cluster 12 (Il12a+/Olfr558+/Olfr78+/Tac1+) expressing short-chain fatty acid sensors. These represent distinct subpopulations with different physiological roles.
evaluation: Reviewers describe the transcriptomic data as 'solid' and note it 'will guide future research,' indicating acceptance of the proximal colon EC cell heterogeneity. No specific concerns were raised about these cluster characterizations or their functional annotations.

result: Distal colonic EC cells (clusters 13-14) express Ascl1 (a neural fate commitment transcription factor) exclusively in Tph1+ cells, conserved in human rectum. These cells are enriched for neuronal genes and GO terms related to neuron projection morphogenesis, axon development, and cilium assembly. Morphologically, they exhibit unique long basal processes (50-100 μm) with 5-HT concentrated in the processes, and express cilia markers (Foxj1, Dnah9, IFT88).
evaluation: Reviewers describe the data as 'solid' and note the manuscript focuses on 'a EC-cluster in the distal colon, which expresses Piezo2, rendering these cells mechanosensitive,' implicitly accepting the neuronal characterization of distal colonic EC cells. The transcriptomic data showing neuronal features are part of the accepted 'granular' dataset.

result: Piezo2, encoding a mechanosensitive ion channel, was identified in almost all distal colonic EC cells by scRNA-seq and validated by smRNA-FISH to be robustly expressed in Ascl1+/Tph1+ cells in the epithelial layer. qPCR showed up to 360-fold enrichment in distal colon GFP+ cells compared to other gut regions. Piezo2 was not detected in EC cells from proximal colon or small intestine. A subpopulation co-expresses Piezo2 with Foxj1 and Olfr78, suggesting mechanosensory function.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly state the manuscript focuses on 'a EC-cluster in the distal colon, which expresses Piezo2, rendering these cells mechanosensitive' and describe the data as 'solid.' One reviewer notes 'Piezo2 has been implicated in mechanosensitive serotonin release previously' but states 'the data are solid and emphasize the importance of mechanosensitive serotonin release for colonic propulsion,' indicating acceptance of the Piezo2 expression characterization.

result: Chemogenetic activation of Piezo2+ cells using CNO in Piezo2-CHRM3* mice led to robust serotonin release (2.1-fold elevation in serum, 1.9-fold from isolated mCitrine+/Epcam+ cells), increased fecal pellet output, and significantly accelerated colon motility (bead expulsion time shortened from 7.24 to 1.16 min). No effects were observed in wild-type or control mice.
evaluation: Reviewers describe the data as 'solid' and note the authors 'employ new tools to establish a role of mechanosensitive EC cells for colonic and thus total intestinal transit.' The chemogenetic activation experiments are part of the accepted evidence demonstrating the functional role of Piezo2+ cells in colonic motility.

result: Diphtheria toxin-mediated ablation of Piezo2+ cells in Piezo2-DTR mice resulted in profound co-depletion of Piezo2 and Tph1 transcripts and substantial loss of 5-HT+ cells in the distal colon (validated by smRNA-FISH and immunofluorescence), while maintaining general epithelial architecture. This led to 42% reduction in fecal pellet output, substantial delay in bead expulsion (36.9 vs 8.2 min), small but significant slowdown in small intestine transit, and delayed whole gut transit time (181.8 vs 136.7 min).
evaluation: Reviewers state 'a role for Piezo2 expressing cells for colonic transit is convincingly demonstrated' and describe the data as 'solid.' The diphtheria toxin ablation experiments are explicitly accepted as part of the evidence establishing the functional importance of Piezo2+ EC cells for intestinal motility.

result: Conditional gut epithelial-specific Piezo2 knockout (Villin-cre;Piezo2fl/fl) resulted in Piezo2 depletion from distal colon epithelium (validated by qPCR and smRNA-FISH) without affecting Tph1/Chga levels or basal serotonin. Residual Piezo2 signals were observed in some Tph1+ cells and lamina propria remained unaltered. This led to significant slowing of bead expulsion (33.7 vs 9.25 min), prolonged whole gut transit (182 vs 146 min), and shorter colon transit distance (51.2% vs 72.1%), with no effect on small intestinal transit. The authors conclude that Piezo2+/Ascl1+/Tph1+ cells are required for normal colon motility.
evaluation: Reviewers state 'a role for Piezo2 expressing cells for colonic transit is convincingly demonstrated' using 'conditional gut epithelial specific Piezo2 knock-out.' The data are described as 'solid,' and the conclusion about Piezo2+ cells being required for normal colon motility is accepted as part of the manuscript's core findings.

result: Regional transcription factors (Pitx2, Osr2, Hox genes) showed preferential enrichment along the gut axis, with Hox genes observed only in the colon and Hoxb13 specifically in the distal colon. This pattern was largely conserved in human gut mucosa, with OSR2 and HOXB13 preferentially enriched in human ileum and rectum, respectively.
evaluation: Reviewers describe the transcriptomic data as 'solid' and 'more granular than previous data sets,' indicating acceptance of the regional transcription factor patterns. The conservation in human samples strengthens the findings, and no concerns were raised about these observations.

result: The authors identified and validated by smRNA-FISH several cluster-specific nutrient and chemical sensors in different EEC cell types: Cnr1 in K cells, Asic5 in delta cells, Gper1 in K cells, Stra6 in distal colonic L cells, and Gpbar1 in proximal/distal colonic L cells (not EC cells). Ffar1 was found in almost all Cck+ cells and Gcg+ L cells, while Ffar2 was widely observed in all EEC cells except K cells. Almost all molecular sensors were confined to EEC cells with little expression in other epithelial cell types.
evaluation: Reviewers describe the transcriptomic data as 'solid' and note it 'will guide future research,' indicating acceptance of the sensor molecule characterization across different EEC cell types. No concerns were raised about the identification or validation of these cluster-specific sensors.

result: Htr4 (encoding the 5-HT4 receptor) was selectively expressed by epithelium in the deep crypts of distal colon, and the long basal processes of EC cells filled with 5-HT extend toward the base of the crypts where Htr4 is preferentially expressed.
evaluation: Reviewers describe the data as 'solid' and accept the characterization of distal colonic EC cells. This observation about Htr4 localization and EC cell process orientation is part of the accepted anatomical and molecular characterization of these cells.

result: 15.9% of Piezo2 CKO mice died around 21-34 days after birth, with affected animals presenting 42% reduction in body weight and runt body size by the time of humane euthanasia.
evaluation: Reviewers describe the data as 'solid' and accept the conditional knockout experiments. While this mortality phenotype is noted, no concerns were raised about its validity or interpretation as part of the Piezo2 loss-of-function characterization.

result: Piezo2 signals were observed in the lamina propria throughout the intestine, and Piezo2 was previously detected in a subset of sensory DRG neurons innervating the colon. The authors suggest both distal colonic EC cells and sensory DRG neurons may contribute to mechanosensory sensing and motility control.
evaluation: One reviewer notes 'the nature of the mechanical stimulus or the stimulus-secretion coupling downstream of Piezo2 activation is not clear,' suggesting uncertainty about the mechanistic details. While the expression of Piezo2 in both EC cells and DRG neurons is accepted, the relative contributions and interactions between these cell types remain unclear.

result: Background claims about EC cells constituting <1% of intestinal epithelium, producing >90% of body's serotonin, modulating physiological functions, and dysregulation being implicated in various diseases (GI, cardiovascular, osteoporosis, SIDS, psychiatric disorders).
evaluation: These are well-established background facts supported by multiple literature citations. Reviewers do not question these foundational claims, which provide context for the study's importance.

result: Background claims about EEC cell lineage (all derive from Neurog3+ cells) and established markers (Chga/Chgb for EC cells, Tac1 for crypt EC cells, Sct for villus EC cells).
evaluation: These are established facts from prior literature that reviewers do not question. They provide necessary context for the cluster annotations and validation approaches used in the study.

result: Background claims about previously reported findings: Olfr78/Olfr558 enrichment in colon, 5-HT causing colorectal propulsion, and gut's defensive role in expelling toxins via 5-HT release.
evaluation: These are confirmatory findings or established facts from prior literature. One reviewer notes 'some of these data are confirmative of previous reports' but states 'the data are solid,' indicating acceptance of these observations as supporting context.

result: Validation of cluster 6 findings in an independent Neurod1-tdTomato scRNA-seq dataset, showing a discrete Cck+/Tph1+ cluster with high levels of Cck, Sct, Tph1, Ghrl, Gcg, and Nts. Oc3 and key signature genes from cluster 6 were specifically identified in this population, with ~99% of Casr+/Mc4r+ cells co-expressing pathogen/toxin recognition genes.
evaluation: Reviewers describe the transcriptomic data as 'solid,' and the validation in an independent dataset strengthens the cluster 6 characterization. No concerns were raised about this cross-dataset validation.
